    ### Euclidean Cluster Extraction with DON
    
    Source: https://github.com/pointcloudlibrary/pcl/blob/master/doc/advanced/content/don_segmentation.md
    
    This code snippet shows how to use EuclideanClusterExtraction after applying the DON segmentation to extract individual clusters from the point cloud.
    
    ```cpp
    std::cout << "Clustering using EuclideanClusterExtraction with tolerance <= " << segradius << "..." << std::endl;
    
    pcl::search::KdTree<PointNormal>::Ptr segtree (new pcl::search::KdTree<PointNormal>);
    segtree->setInputCloud (doncloud);
    
    std::vector<pcl::PointIndices> cluster_indices;
    pcl::EuclideanClusterExtraction<PointNormal> ec;
    
    ec.setClusterTolerance (segradius);
    ec.setMinClusterSize (50);
    ec.setMaxClusterSize (100000);
    ec.setSearchMethod (segtree);
    ec.setInputCloud (doncloud);
    ec.extract (cluster_indices);
    
    int j = 0;
    for (const auto& cluster : cluster_indices)
    {
      pcl::PointCloud<PointNormal>::Ptr cloud_cluster_don (new pcl::PointCloud<PointNormal>);
      for (const auto& idx : cluster.indices)
      {
        cloud_cluster_don->points.push_back ((*doncloud)[idx]);
      }
    
      cloud_cluster_don->width = cloud_cluster_don->size ();
      cloud_cluster_don->height = 1;
      cloud_cluster_don->is_dense = true;
    
      //Save cluster
      std::cout << "PointCloud representing the Cluster: " << cloud_cluster_don->size () << " data points." << std::endl;
      std::stringstream ss;
      ss << "don_cluster_" << j << ".pcd";
      writer.write<pcl::PointNormal> (ss.str (), *cloud_cluster_don, false);
      ++j;
    }
    }

    The Moment of Inertia estimation feature allows for the geometric analysis of point clouds. > RGB-D input → carton instances → label/barcode/OCR → 3D dimensions and pose → collision-checked grasp

There are projects that come close, but they either use learned segmentation, target different objects/robots, or are research demonstrations rather than reusable production systems.

## The classical pipeline is established

Your preferred approach—support-plane removal, clustering, box fitting, and projection—is not something we would be inventing. It is effectively a canonical tabletop-object segmentation pipeline. :codex-annotation{index="1"}

PCL has long provided exactly these stages:

1. Filter or downsample the cloud.
2. Estimate normals.
3. Find the support plane using sample consensus/RANSAC.
4. Remove the plane.
5. Optionally extract points inside a polygonal prism above the plane.
6. Apply Euclidean clustering.
7. Compute bounding boxes and geometric features for each cluster.

PCL’s original architecture explicitly includes filtering, sample-consensus model fitting, polygonal-prism extraction, and clustering, and its current documentation exposes those components independently. [PCL overview paper](https://pointclouds.org/assets/pdf/pcl_icra2011.pdf), [PCL segmentation documentation](https://pointclouds.org/documentation/group__segmentation.html)

Open3D provides a more convenient Python version of most of the same machinery:

- RGB-D image to point cloud
- voxel downsampling
- plane RANSAC with `segment_plane`
- DBSCAN clustering with `cluster_dbscan`
- normal estimation
- axis-aligned and oriented bounding boxes

See the official [Open3D point-cloud tutorial](https://github.com/isl-org/open3d/blob/main/docs/jupyter/geometry/pointcloud.ipynb).

So we would be writing orchestration and carton-specific reasoning—not implementations of RANSAC, nearest-neighbor clustering, point-cloud storage, or basic bounding boxes.

## The closest complete project I found

The nearest open-source match is [YoloSegment-2D-to-3D-RebotARM_Pick_and_Place](https://github.com/danieldoradotalaveron-rb/YoloSegment-2D-to-3D-RebotARM_Pick_and_Place).

It already performs:

- Intel RealSense RGB-D capture
- 2D instance segmentation
- mask lifting into 3D
- per-frame RANSAC table-plane estimation
- table-aligned oriented bounding boxes
- temporal pose stabilization
- hand–eye transformation into the robot base frame
- publication as ROS 2 `Detection3DArray`
- MoveIt approach, descent, grasp, lift, and placement

Architecturally, that is very close to what we want. It even addresses a useful subtlety: symmetric objects should not be assigned an arbitrary, unstable yaw.

However:

- It uses trained YOLO segmentation rather than classical depth segmentation.
- Its demonstration classes are corks, pom-poms, and a lighter.
- It is tied to a specific reBot arm configuration.
- It has only a small development history, so I would treat it as a reference implementation, not a dependency around which to design the whole system.
- It does not solve carton label interpretation or medicine identity.

The useful parts to study are its interfaces, temporal stability checks, table-relative bounding boxes, hand–eye calibration, and how it passes perception results to MoveIt.

## What already exists at each stage

| Stage | Existing solution | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| RGB-D decoding and calibration | Our current reader and projector | Keep ours |
| Point-cloud construction | Open3D or PCL | Reuse |
| Workspace filtering | Open3D/PCL pass-through and voxel filters | Reuse |
| Plane detection | Open3D `segment_plane`, PCL `SACSegmentation` | Reuse |
| Points above a shelf/table | PCL `ExtractPolygonalPrismData`, or a short signed-distance filter | Reuse concept; thin Python code |
| Object clustering | Open3D DBSCAN or PCL Euclidean clustering | Reuse |
| Outlier removal | Open3D/PCL statistical and radius filters | Reuse |
| Bounding boxes | Open3D/PCL AABB and OBB | Reuse initially |
| Constrained carton fitting | Generic cuboid fitting exists, but carton-specific constraints help | Adapt/build a thin layer |
| 3D-to-color projection | Our calibrated mapping | Keep ours |
| Barcode decoding | ZXing, ZBar, OpenCV barcode module | Reuse |
| OCR | PaddleOCR, Tesseract, EasyOCR | Reuse |
| Grasp candidates | Analytic box grasps, GPD, VGN, GraspNet | Start analytic; evaluate learned methods later |
| Robot planning | MoveIt Task Constructor | Reuse |

For generic cuboid RANSAC, [pyRANSAC-3D](https://github.com/leomariga/pyRANSAC-3D) is relevant. I would test it, but not assume it will directly solve our problem. A RealSense normally sees only one to three carton faces, with noisy or missing depth around edges. A generic unconstrained cuboid fitter may become unstable under those conditions.

For execution, [MoveIt Task Constructor](https://github.com/moveit/moveit_task_constructor) already models the grasp sequence—generation, approach, inverse kinematics, collision checks, attachment, lift, transfer, and placement. We should not reproduce that machinery.

## Where custom development is still justified

The important custom part is domain knowledge about cartons and the physical workspace.

### 1. Shelf rather than generic tabletop reasoning

A tabletop system often assumes:

- one dominant horizontal plane;
- objects clearly separated from that plane;
- space above the plane is unobstructed.

A medicine shelf may instead contain:

- horizontal shelves and a vertical back panel;
- boxes touching the back panel;
- boxes touching one another;
- boxes standing, lying flat, or leaning;
- narrow gaps and occlusions;
- depth shadows at package edges.

Therefore, plane removal alone will not always separate the cartons. Adjacent packages can form one depth cluster.

We will likely use known shelf geometry or plane-normal constraints:

- identify horizontal shelf planes;
- identify or exclude the vertical back plane;
- retain points inside a bounded shelf volume;
- cluster remaining points;
- split merged clusters using depth discontinuities, color edges, or competing cuboid hypotheses.

That is application-specific glue, not reinvention of the underlying algorithms.

### 2. Better carton boxes

A raw PCA-oriented bounding box can jump between orientations or underestimate dimensions when only the front and side are visible.

For cartons, a better estimator can enforce:

- mutually perpendicular faces;
- one axis parallel to the shelf normal or gravity;
- dimensions within plausible package ranges;
- visible points lying on cuboid surfaces;
- the rear face terminating at or near the shelf back plane;
- temporal consistency across frames.

This remains understandable: every score and rejected hypothesis can be displayed.

### 3. Grasp reasoning

We probably do not need a general learned grasp network initially. Once a carton cuboid is known, grasp generation is straightforward:

- enumerate reachable front, side, or top pinch grasps;
- reject faces that are occluded or against the shelf;
- require enough free gripper clearance;
- avoid grasping over critical label/barcode regions if desired;
- check jaw width against the estimated carton dimension;
- rank by surface support, approach clearance, and distance from edges;
- send surviving candidates to MoveIt for IK and collision checking.

General grasp systems such as [GPD](https://github.com/atenpas/gpd) and [VGN](https://github.com/ethz-asl/vgn) already exist, but they introduce learned scoring and additional integration. GraspNet is another option, though its official baseline carries non-commercial-use restrictions. They are useful comparison points after we establish an analytic baseline.

## What I recommend we build

Use Open3D for the first implementation because this project is currently Python/NumPy based and we want to inspect each intermediate result. PCL remains attractive later if this moves into a high-rate C++ ROS node. The library documentation check reinforced this choice: Open3D exposes nearly all of our first-stage pipeline without requiring a ROS/PCL build.

The first detector should be something like:

```text
rotated depth + calibration
        ↓
calibrated 3D point cloud
        ↓
workspace/depth crop
        ↓
voxel downsampling + outlier removal
        ↓
support-plane detection
        ↓
points within shelf volume and in front of plane
        ↓
spatial clustering
        ↓
box/cuboid estimation
        ↓
project box edges and cluster masks into RGB
```

Crucially, the viewer should let us toggle:

- raw point cloud;
- plane inliers;
- rejected points;
- individual clusters;
- fitted bounding boxes;
- projected RGB outlines;
- numerical dimensions and fit residuals.

That gives us a completely inspectable baseline. Later, a YOLO or segmentation model can replace or assist only the weak stage—probably separating touching packages—without replacing calibration, geometry, dimensions, pose, or grasp validation.

So the bottom line is: **we are not reinventing the point-cloud pipeline**. We would be assembling mature components and contributing the relatively small but valuable portion that existing generic libraries do not know: “this scene is a shelf, these objects are rectangular medicine cartons, and this gripper must safely extract one.”

    """Interactively step through an RGB-D ``.db3`` recording.
    
    Run with::
    
        python main.py recording.db3
    
    The images are shown in a Matplotlib window while navigation commands are read
    from the terminal.
    """
    
    from __future__ import annotations
    
    import argparse
    from pathlib import Path
    
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    import numpy as np
    from matplotlib.axes import Axes
    from matplotlib.backend_bases import MouseEvent
    from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
    from matplotlib.text import Text
    
    from rgbd_db3_reader import (
        DepthColorProjector,
        ProjectionMetrics,
        RGBDDB3Reader,
        RGBDFrame,
    )
    
    
    class LinkedPixelHighlighter:
        """Show calibrated depth/color pixel correspondences."""
    
        def __init__(self, axes: np.ndarray, projector: DepthColorProjector) -> None:
            self.axes = tuple(axes)
            self.projector = projector
            self._shapes: dict[Axes, tuple[int, int]] = {}
            self._depth_meters: np.ndarray | None = None
            self._artists: dict[Axes, tuple[Line2D, Line2D, Line2D, Text]] = {}
    
            figure = self.axes[0].figure
            figure.canvas.mpl_connect("motion_notify_event", self._on_mouse)
            figure.canvas.mpl_connect("button_press_event", self._on_mouse)
    
        def reset(
            self,
            frame: RGBDFrame,
            depth_meters: np.ndarray | None,
        ) -> ProjectionMetrics | None:
            """Recreate the overlay artists after the axes have been cleared."""
    
            color_axis, depth_axis = self.axes
            self._shapes.clear()
            self._artists.clear()
            self._depth_meters = depth_meters
    
            if frame.color is not None:
                self._shapes[color_axis] = frame.color.shape[:2]
                self._artists[color_axis] = self._make_artists(color_axis)
            if frame.depth is not None:
                self._shapes[depth_axis] = frame.depth.shape[:2]
                self._artists[depth_axis] = self._make_artists(depth_axis)
    
            if frame.color is None or self._depth_meters is None:
                return None
            return self.projector.build(self._depth_meters, frame.color.shape[:2])
    
        @staticmethod
        def _make_artists(axis: Axes) -> tuple[Line2D, Line2D, Line2D, Text]:
            style = {"color": "magenta", "linewidth": 1.0, "visible": False}
            vertical = axis.axvline(0, **style)
            horizontal = axis.axhline(0, **style)
            marker = axis.plot(
                0,
                0,
                marker="o",
                markersize=7,
                markerfacecolor="none",
                markeredgecolor="white",
                markeredgewidth=1.5,
                linestyle="none",
                visible=False,
            )[0]
            label = axis.text(
                0.02,
                0.98,
                "",
                transform=axis.transAxes,
                ha="left",
                va="top",
                color="white",
                fontsize=9,
                bbox={"facecolor": "black", "alpha": 0.65, "edgecolor": "none"},
                visible=False,
            )
            return vertical, horizontal, marker, label
    
        def _on_mouse(self, event: MouseEvent) -> None:
            source_axis = event.inaxes
            if source_axis not in self._shapes or event.xdata is None or event.ydata is None:
                return
    
            source_height, source_width = self._shapes[source_axis]
            source_x = min(max(round(event.xdata), 0), source_width - 1)
            source_y = min(max(round(event.ydata), 0), source_height - 1)
    
            color_axis, depth_axis = self.axes
            self._show_pixel(source_axis, source_x, source_y)
            if source_axis is depth_axis:
                corresponding = self.projector.projected_color_pixel(source_x, source_y)
                target_axis = color_axis
            else:
                corresponding = self.projector.nearest_depth_pixel(source_x, source_y)
                target_axis = depth_axis
    
            if corresponding is None or target_axis not in self._artists:
                self._hide_pixel(target_axis)
            else:
                self._show_pixel(target_axis, *corresponding)
    
            source_axis.figure.canvas.draw_idle()
    
        def _show_pixel(self, axis: Axes, x: int, y: int) -> None:
            vertical, horizontal, marker, label = self._artists[axis]
            vertical.set_xdata([x, x])
            horizontal.set_ydata([y, y])
            marker.set_data([x], [y])
    
            text = f"pixel ({x}, {y})"
            if axis is self.axes[1] and self._depth_meters is not None:
                depth = float(self._depth_meters[y, x])
                text += f"\ndepth: {depth:.3f} m" if depth > 0 else "\ndepth: invalid"
            label.set_text(text)
    
            for artist in (vertical, horizontal, marker, label):
                artist.set_visible(True)
    
        def _hide_pixel(self, axis: Axes) -> None:
            if axis not in self._artists:
                return
            for artist in self._artists[axis]:
                artist.set_visible(False)
    
    
    def show_frame(
        frame: RGBDFrame,
        axes: np.ndarray,
        highlighter: LinkedPixelHighlighter,
    ) -> ProjectionMetrics | None:
        """Draw one RGB-D frame in the existing Matplotlib window."""
    
        color_axis, depth_axis = axes
        color_axis.clear()
        depth_axis.clear()
    
        if frame.color is None:
            color_axis.text(0.5, 0.5, "No paired color frame", ha="center", va="center")
        else:
            color = frame.color
            # Matplotlib accepts grayscale, RGB, and RGBA arrays directly.
            color_axis.imshow(color, cmap="gray" if color.ndim == 2 else None)
        color_axis.set_title("Color")
        color_axis.axis("off")
    
        depth_meters = frame.depth_meters
        if depth_meters is None:
            depth_axis.text(0.5, 0.5, "No depth frame", ha="center", va="center")
        else:
            # Mask zero values, which normally mean that no depth was measured.
            depth_axis.imshow(np.ma.masked_less_equal(depth_meters, 0), cmap="turbo")
        depth_axis.set_title("Depth (meters)")
        depth_axis.axis("off")
    
        metrics = highlighter.reset(frame, depth_meters)
        timing_text = ""
        if metrics is not None:
            throughput = metrics.valid_points / metrics.total_ms / 1000
            timing_text = f"  |  map {metrics.total_ms:.1f} ms"
            print(
                f"frame {frame.index}: reprojection {metrics.total_ms:.2f} ms "
                f"(project {metrics.projection_ms:.2f} ms, "
                f"z-buffer {metrics.z_buffer_ms:.2f} ms, "
                f"{metrics.valid_points:,} valid, {metrics.projected_points:,} in frame, "
                f"{throughput:.2f} Mpoints/s)"
            )
        color_axis.figure.suptitle(
            f"Frame {frame.index}  |  timestamp {frame.timestamp_ns / 1e9:.3f} s{timing_text}"
        )
        color_axis.figure.canvas.draw_idle()
        plt.pause(0.001)
        return metrics
    
    
    def browse_recording(bag_path: Path, *, rotate_clockwise: bool = True) -> None:
        """Open *bag_path* and browse its paired frames using terminal commands."""
    
        with RGBDDB3Reader(bag_path, rotate_clockwise=rotate_clockwise) as reader:
            if len(reader) == 0:
                print("The recording contains no paired frames.")
                return
    
            fps_text = "unknown" if reader.fps is None else f"{reader.fps:.2f}"
            print(f"Loaded {len(reader)} frames (approximately {fps_text} FPS).")
            orientation = "90 degrees clockwise" if rotate_clockwise else "native"
            print(f"Processing orientation: {orientation}.")
            print("Commands: Enter/n = next, p = previous, <number> = jump, q = quit")
            print("Move or click over either image to highlight the corresponding pixels.")
    
            projector = reader.make_projector()
    
            _, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 6))
            highlighter = LinkedPixelHighlighter(axes, projector)
            plt.show(block=False)
            index = 0
            timing_samples: list[float] = []
    
            while plt.fignum_exists(axes[0].figure.number):
                reader.seek(index)
                ok, frame = reader.read()
                if not ok or frame is None:
                    break
                metrics = show_frame(frame, axes, highlighter)
                if metrics is not None:
                    timing_samples.append(metrics.total_ms)
    
                command = input(f"frame {index}/{len(reader) - 1}> ").strip().lower()
                if command in {"q", "quit", "exit"}:
                    break
                if command in {"", "n", "next"}:
                    index = min(index + 1, len(reader) - 1)
                elif command in {"p", "prev", "previous"}:
                    index = max(index - 1, 0)
                else:
                    try:
                        requested_index = int(command)
                    except ValueError:
                        print("Unknown command. Use Enter/n, p, a frame number, or q.")
                        continue
    
                    if 0 <= requested_index < len(reader):
                        index = requested_index
                    else:
                        print(f"Frame must be between 0 and {len(reader) - 1}.")
    
            if timing_samples:
                samples = np.asarray(timing_samples)
                print(
                    f"Reprojection summary ({len(samples)} builds): "
                    f"mean={samples.mean():.2f} ms, median={np.median(samples):.2f} ms, "
                    f"p95={np.percentile(samples, 95):.2f} ms"
                )
    
        plt.close("all")
    
    
    def main() -> None:
        parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Browse frames in an RGB-D db3 recording.")
        parser.add_argument("bag", type=Path, help="path to the .db3 recording")
        parser.add_argument(
            "--native-orientation",
            action="store_true",
            help="do not rotate frames and calibration clockwise",
        )
        args = parser.parse_args()
        browse_recording(args.bag, rotate_clockwise=not args.native_orientation)
    
    
    if __name__ == "__main__":
        main()

    class DepthColorProjector:
        """Build depth/color pixel correspondences in the calibration's coordinates."""
    
        def __init__(
            self,
            depth_intrinsics: CameraIntrinsics,
            color_intrinsics: CameraIntrinsics,
            depth_to_color: RigidTransform,
        ) -> None:
            self.depth_intrinsics = depth_intrinsics
            self.color_intrinsics = color_intrinsics
            self.rotation = np.asarray(depth_to_color.rotation, dtype=np.float32)
            self.translation = np.asarray(depth_to_color.translation, dtype=np.float32)
            self.depth_to_color_x = np.empty((0, 0), dtype=np.int32)
            self.depth_to_color_y = np.empty((0, 0), dtype=np.int32)
            self.color_to_depth = np.empty((0, 0), dtype=np.int32)
            self._depth_shape = (0, 0)
            self._ray_x = np.empty((0, 0), dtype=np.float32)
            self._ray_y = np.empty((0, 0), dtype=np.float32)
    
        @staticmethod
        def _scaled_parameters(
            intrinsics: CameraIntrinsics,
            shape: tuple[int, int],
        ) -> tuple[float, float, float, float]:
            height, width = shape
            if height <= 0 or width <= 0:
                raise ValueError(f"invalid image shape: {shape}")
            calibrated_aspect = intrinsics.width / intrinsics.height
            actual_aspect = width / height
            if not np.isclose(actual_aspect, calibrated_aspect, rtol=1e-3):
                raise ValueError(
                    f"image shape {shape} is incompatible with calibrated size "
                    f"({intrinsics.height}, {intrinsics.width}); check the rotation setting"
                )
            scale_x = width / intrinsics.width
            scale_y = height / intrinsics.height
            fx = intrinsics.fx * scale_x
            fy = intrinsics.fy * scale_y
            cx = (intrinsics.cx + 0.5) * scale_x - 0.5
            cy = (intrinsics.cy + 0.5) * scale_y - 0.5
            return fx, fy, cx, cy
    
        def _prepare_depth_rays(self, shape: tuple[int, int]) -> None:
            if shape == self._depth_shape:
                return
            height, width = shape
            fx, fy, cx, cy = self._scaled_parameters(self.depth_intrinsics, shape)
            pixel_x, pixel_y = np.meshgrid(
                np.arange(width, dtype=np.float32),
                np.arange(height, dtype=np.float32),
            )
            self._ray_x = (pixel_x - cx) / fx
            self._ray_y = (pixel_y - cy) / fy
            self._depth_shape = shape
    
        def build(
            self,
            depth_meters: np.ndarray,
            color_shape: tuple[int, int],
        ) -> ProjectionMetrics:
            """Build forward and z-buffered inverse lookup maps for one frame."""
    
            started = perf_counter()
            depth_shape = depth_meters.shape
            self._prepare_depth_rays(depth_shape)
            color_height, color_width = color_shape
            color_fx, color_fy, color_cx, color_cy = self._scaled_parameters(
                self.color_intrinsics, color_shape
            )
    
            depth = np.asarray(depth_meters, dtype=np.float32)
            depth_flat = depth.ravel()
            valid_indices = np.flatnonzero(np.isfinite(depth_flat) & (depth_flat > 0))
            z_depth = depth_flat[valid_indices]
            x_depth = self._ray_x.ravel()[valid_indices] * z_depth
            y_depth = self._ray_y.ravel()[valid_indices] * z_depth
    
            points_depth = np.column_stack((x_depth, y_depth, z_depth))
            points_color = points_depth @ self.rotation.T + self.translation
            z_color = points_color[:, 2]
            with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
                projected_x = np.rint(color_fx * points_color[:, 0] / z_color + color_cx)
                projected_y = np.rint(color_fy * points_color[:, 1] / z_color + color_cy)
    
            inside = (
                np.isfinite(projected_x)
                & np.isfinite(projected_y)
                & (z_color > 0)
                & (projected_x >= 0)
                & (projected_x < color_width)
                & (projected_y >= 0)
                & (projected_y < color_height)
            )
            source_indices = valid_indices[inside]
            color_x = projected_x[inside].astype(np.int32)
            color_y = projected_y[inside].astype(np.int32)
            visible_z = z_color[inside]
    
            self.depth_to_color_x = np.full(depth_shape, -1, dtype=np.int32)
            self.depth_to_color_y = np.full(depth_shape, -1, dtype=np.int32)
            self.depth_to_color_x.ravel()[source_indices] = color_x
            self.depth_to_color_y.ravel()[source_indices] = color_y
            projected_at = perf_counter()
    
            destination_indices = color_y * color_width + color_x
            z_buffer = np.full(color_height * color_width, np.inf, dtype=np.float32)
            np.minimum.at(z_buffer, destination_indices, visible_z)
            frontmost = visible_z <= z_buffer[destination_indices] + 1e-6
            self.color_to_depth = np.full(color_shape, -1, dtype=np.int32)
            self.color_to_depth.ravel()[destination_indices[frontmost]] = source_indices[frontmost]
            finished = perf_counter()
    
            return ProjectionMetrics(
                total_ms=(finished - started) * 1000,
                projection_ms=(projected_at - started) * 1000,
                z_buffer_ms=(finished - projected_at) * 1000,
                valid_points=len(valid_indices),
                projected_points=len(source_indices),
            )
    
        def projected_color_pixel(self, depth_x: int, depth_y: int) -> tuple[int, int] | None:
            """Return the projected color pixel for one depth pixel."""
    
            color_x = int(self.depth_to_color_x[depth_y, depth_x])
            color_y = int(self.depth_to_color_y[depth_y, depth_x])
            return None if color_x < 0 or color_y < 0 else (color_x, color_y)
    
        def nearest_depth_pixel(
            self,
            color_x: int,
            color_y: int,
            *,
            radius: int = 3,
        ) -> tuple[int, int] | None:
            """Find the nearest projected depth sample around a color pixel."""
    
            height, width = self.color_to_depth.shape
            x0, x1 = max(0, color_x - radius), min(width, color_x + radius + 1)
            y0, y1 = max(0, color_y - radius), min(height, color_y + radius + 1)
            window = self.color_to_depth[y0:y1, x0:x1]
            candidate_y, candidate_x = np.nonzero(window >= 0)
            if not len(candidate_x):
                return None
            distances = (candidate_x + x0 - color_x) ** 2 + (candidate_y + y0 - color_y) ** 2
            nearest = int(np.argmin(distances))
            depth_index = int(window[candidate_y[nearest], candidate_x[nearest]])
            depth_width = self.depth_to_color_x.shape[1]
            return depth_index % depth_width, depth_index // depth_width

    ## Voxel Downsampling
    
    ### Description

    ### Method

    ### Description
    Estimates normals for each point in a point cloud using covariance analysis on neighboring points.
    
    ### Method
    `estimate_normals`
    
    ### Parameters
    - `search_param` (open3d.geometry.KDTreeSearchParamHybrid): Search parameters for neighbor finding. The `radius` parameter specifies the search radius, and `max_nn` limits the number of nearest neighbors considered.

    ```

    ### Hash-based deterministic voxel downsampling
    
    Source: https://github.com/isl-org/open3d/blob/main/cpp/open3d/t/geometry/PointCloud.cpp
    
    VoxelDownSample implements deterministic feature processing by: (1) discretizing point positions into integer voxel coordinates, (2) inserting them into a core::HashSet to obtain deterministic insertion masks marking the first occurrence per unique voxel, (3) remapping per-point voxel slots to dense indices, and (4) accumulating attributes via IndexAdd_ followed by mean division. The HashSet guarantees deterministic output: same input always produces the same voxel assignment.
    
    ```cpp
    PointCloud PointCloud::VoxelDownSample(double voxel_size,
                                           const std::string& reduction) const {
        if (voxel_size <= 0) {
            utility::LogError("voxel_size must be positive.");
        }
        if (reduction != "mean") {
            utility::LogError("Reduction can only be 'mean' for VoxelDownSample.");
        }
    
        // Discretize voxels.
        core::Tensor voxeld = GetPointPositions() / voxel_size;
        core::Tensor voxeli = voxeld.Floor().To(core::Int64);
    
        // Map discrete voxels to indices.
        core::HashSet voxeli_hashset(voxeli.GetLength(), core::Int64, {3}, device_);
    
        // Insertion pass: masks==true marks the first occurrence (one per unique
        // voxel); the returned buf_indices are gather indices into the hash buffer.
        core::Tensor insert_buf_indices, insert_masks;
        voxeli_hashset.Insert(voxeli, insert_buf_indices, insert_masks);
    
        int64_t num_points = voxeli.GetLength();
        int64_t num_voxels = voxeli_hashset.Size();
    
        // buf_indices are not guaranteed dense on SYCL; relabel to [0, num_voxels).
        core::Tensor remap = core::Tensor::Zeros({voxeli_hashset.GetCapacity()},
                                                 core::Int64, device_);
        core::Tensor unique_slots =
                insert_buf_indices.IndexGet({insert_masks}).To(core::Int64);
        remap.IndexSet({unique_slots},
                       core::Tensor::Arange(int64_t(0), num_voxels, int64_t(1),
                                            core::Int64, device_));
    
        // Find pass: per-point gather index of its voxel slot, then relabel dense.
        core::Tensor index_map_point2voxel, masks;
        voxeli_hashset.Find(voxeli, index_map_point2voxel, masks);
        index_map_point2voxel =
                remap.IndexGet({index_map_point2voxel.To(core::Int64)});
    
        // Count the number of points in each voxel.
        auto voxel_num_points =
                core::Tensor::Zeros({num_voxels}, core::Float32, device_);
        voxel_num_points.IndexAdd_(
                /*dim*/ 0, index_map_point2voxel,
                core::Tensor::Ones({num_points}, core::Float32, device_));
    
        // Create a new point cloud.
        PointCloud pcd_down(device_);
        for (auto& kv : point_attr_) {
            auto point_attr = kv.second;
    
            std::string attr_string = kv.first;
            auto attr_dtype = point_attr.GetDtype();
    
            core::SizeVector attr_shape = point_attr.GetShape();
            attr_shape[0] = num_voxels;
            auto voxel_attr =
                    core::Tensor::Zeros(attr_shape, core::Float32, device_);
            if (reduction == "mean") {
                voxel_attr.IndexAdd_(0, index_map_point2voxel,
                                     point_attr.To(core::Float32));
                voxel_attr /= voxel_num_points.View({-1, 1});
                voxel_attr = voxel_attr.To(attr_dtype);
            } else {
                utility::LogError("Unsupported reduction type {}.", reduction);
            }
            pcd_down.SetPointAttr(attr_string, voxel_attr);
        }
    
        return pcd_down;
    }
    ```
    
    ### Downsampling > Voxel downsampling
    
    Source: https://github.com/isl-org/open3d/blob/main/docs/jupyter/t_geometry/pointcloud.ipynb
    
    Voxel downsampling uses a regular voxel grid to create a uniformly downsampled point cloud from an input point cloud. It is often used as a pre-processing step for many point cloud processing tasks. The algorithm operates in two steps:
    
    1. Points are bucketed into voxels.
    2. Each occupied voxel generates exactly one point by averaging all points inside.

[PCL clustering tutorial](https://pointclouds.org/documentation/tutorials/cluster_extraction.html), [Open3D point-cloud tutorial](https://www.open3d.org/docs/latest/tutorial/geometry/pointcloud.html)

## Processing stages

### 1. Convert depth pixels to 3D

For every valid depth pixel:

```text
Z = depth
X = (u - cx) Z / fx
Y = (v - cy) Z / fy
```

Because the reader already rotates both the depth image and its intrinsics, this happens entirely in the rotated portrait coordinate system. We do not need to undo or redo the rotation.

We retain the original depth-pixel index associated with every 3D point. That allows the final 3D cluster labels to be painted back onto the depth image exactly.

### 2. Apply a workspace filter

Before plane fitting, discard points that clearly cannot belong to the working area:

- invalid or zero depth
- points nearer than approximately `0.25 m`
- points farther than an initially configurable limit, perhaps `1.5–2.0 m`
- optionally, points outside a configurable image rectangle

This is important because “largest plane in the entire camera view” could otherwise be a wall or background surface instead of the table.

Initially, every threshold will be a command-line parameter. We should not bury experimentally chosen values in the code.

### 3. Voxel-downsample while preserving pixel correspondence

Running neighborhood clustering directly on all 342,000 points can be unnecessarily expensive. Open3D provides `voxel_down_sample_and_trace`, which both downsamples the cloud and records which original points contributed to each voxel. [Open3D `PointCloud` API](https://www.open3d.org/docs/release/python_api/open3d.geometry.PointCloud.html)

I would start with a voxel size around:

```text
5 mm
```

This should retain carton-scale geometry while substantially reducing the number of points. The trace information lets us propagate a cluster label from each voxel back to every corresponding depth pixel.

This current API check is useful because it means we do not have to implement our own downsampler or perform hundreds of thousands of nearest-neighbor searches afterward.

### 4. Detect the table using RANSAC

Use Open3D’s:

```python
plane_model, inliers = cloud.segment_plane(
    distance_threshold=...,
    ransac_n=3,
    num_iterations=...,
)
```

An initial plane-distance threshold of approximately `8–12 mm` is reasonable for a D435-class depth image, but we will tune it from the recordings.

RANSAC repeatedly selects three points, fits a plane, and counts how many other points lie near it. The winning plane is returned as:

```text
aX + bY + cZ + d = 0
```

This is highly inspectable. We can display:

- the chosen plane
- the number and percentage of inliers
- the fitting threshold
- the residual distance of every point
- whether the detected plane is geometrically plausible

Open3D’s official example uses this same `segment_plane` and `select_by_index` approach. [Open3D plane-segmentation example](https://github.com/isl-org/open3d/blob/main/docs/jupyter/geometry/pointcloud.ipynb)

### 5. Keep points above the table

We should not merely remove the plane inliers and assume everything else is an object. Instead, calculate each point’s signed perpendicular distance from the table.

After orienting the plane normal toward the camera, retain points approximately:

```text
1 cm to 40 cm above the table
```

This removes:

- the table itself
- geometry below the table
- most distant background points
- noise immediately around the fitted plane

The maximum object height remains configurable.

### 6. Cluster the remaining points

Run Open3D DBSCAN on the surviving downsampled points:

```python
labels = cloud.cluster_dbscan(
    eps=...,
    min_points=...,
)
```

An initial neighborhood radius around `15–25 mm` should be appropriate, with perhaps `20–50` minimum downsampled points. Open3D’s documented example uses this operation and assigns colors from a categorical colormap. [Open3D DBSCAN example](https://github.com/isl-org/open3d/blob/main/docs/jupyter/geometry/pointcloud.ipynb)

We then reject implausible clusters based on:

- too few points
- extremely small physical dimensions
- implausibly large dimensions
- centroid outside the workspace
- insufficient height above the table

For deterministic coloring, clusters can be sorted by their projected horizontal centroid before assigning colors. This avoids random color order changing simply because DBSCAN returned clusters in a different sequence.

### 7. Highlight clusters in both images

For the depth view:

- table pixels: muted gray or translucent red
- noise/unassigned pixels: dark
- object 0: blue
- object 1: orange
- object 2: green
- and so forth

For the color view, use the calibrated lookup arrays already created by `DepthColorProjector`:

```python
projector.depth_to_color_x
projector.depth_to_color_y
projector.color_to_depth
```

Each labeled depth pixel is projected onto its corresponding visible color pixel. The RGB image then receives a transparent color overlay rather than being replaced outright, so printed labels remain readable.

No approximate resizing between the two cameras is necessary.

## Viewer presentation

I suggest three panels:

```text
┌────────────────┬────────────────┬────────────────┐
│ Original color │ Depth + table  │ Colored objects│
│ + RGB overlay  │ plane overlay  │ on depth image │
└────────────────┴────────────────┴────────────────┘
```

Each detected object should also display:

- object number
- number of points
- 3D centroid
- approximate dimensions from an axis-aligned or oriented bounding box

The terminal output would report stage timings:

## Expected first failure modes

The demo will intentionally reveal where the basic geometry stops working:

- If the wall is a larger plane than the table, RANSAC may select the wall. We would add a workspace crop or plane-orientation constraint.
- If two cartons touch, DBSCAN may merge them.
- If an object touches the table with noisy depth, its bottom edge may be removed with the plane.
- Shiny or dark packaging may have missing depth pixels.
- Very small printed details have no role in this stage; label reading comes later from RGB.
- Table clutter such as cables will also be considered objects unless filtered geometrically.

These are useful results rather than hidden errors: the output will show exactly which stage made each decision.

## Recommendation

For the first iteration, use Open3D rather than PCL. It gives us mature RANSAC, DBSCAN, voxel processing, traceable downsampling, and bounding boxes while fitting naturally into the current Python/NumPy code. PCL remains a good option if the final perception node later moves to C++/ROS for tighter real-time constraints.

The first acceptance criterion should be simple:

> On several selected frames, the table is consistently suppressed and each spatially separate above-table object receives a distinct, correctly projected color overlay in both the depth and RGB views.

That will give us a clean foundation for the next problem: splitting touching cartons and fitting stable cuboids.

    pcd.colors = o3d.utility.Vector3dVector(colors[:, :3])
    o3d.visualization.draw_geometries([pcd],
                                      zoom=0.455,
                                      front=[-0.4999, -0.1659, -0.8499],
                                      lookat=[2.1813, 2.0619, 2.0999],
                                      up=[0.1204, -0.9852, 0.1215])
    ```
    
    --------------------------------
    
    ### Get and visualize bounding boxes (AxisAlignedBoundingBox and OrientedBoundingBox)
    
    Source: https://github.com/isl-org/open3d/blob/main/docs/jupyter/geometry/pointcloud.ipynb
    
    Creates an axis-aligned bounding box (red) and an oriented bounding box (green) for the chair point cloud and visualizes them together. Bounding volumes can also be used to crop geometry.
    
    ```python
    aabb = chair.get_axis_aligned_bounding_box()
    aabb.color = (1, 0, 0)
    obb = chair.get_oriented_bounding_box()
    obb.color = (0, 1, 0)
    o3d.visualization.draw_geometries([chair, aabb, obb],
                                      zoom=0.7,
                                      front=[0.5439, -0.2333, -0.8060],
                                      lookat=[2.4615, 2.1331, 1.338],
                                      up=[-0.1781, -0.9708, 0.1608])
    ```

    """Inspectable, geometry-only tabletop object segmentation for RGB-D frames.
    
    The implementation deliberately keeps the calibration and image coordinate
    system supplied by :mod:`rgbd_db3_reader`.  It uses Open3D for voxel
    downsampling, RANSAC plane fitting, and DBSCAN clustering, while retaining the
    source depth-pixel indices needed to turn 3-D clusters back into image masks.
    """
    
    from __future__ import annotations
    
    from dataclasses import dataclass
    from time import perf_counter
    
    import numpy as np
    import open3d as o3d
    
    from rgbd_db3_reader import CameraIntrinsics
    
    
    @dataclass(frozen=True)
    class TabletopSegmentationParameters:
        """Metric thresholds controlling the transparent segmentation pipeline."""
    
        min_depth: float = 0.25
        max_depth: float = 2.0
        voxel_size: float = 0.005
        plane_distance_threshold: float = 0.010
        ransac_iterations: int = 1_000
        object_min_height: float = 0.010
        object_max_height: float = 0.40
        cluster_eps: float = 0.020
        cluster_min_points: int = 20
        min_object_pixels: int = 100
        random_seed: int = 0
    
        def validate(self) -> None:
            """Raise ``ValueError`` for parameter combinations that cannot work."""
    
            if not 0 < self.min_depth < self.max_depth:
                raise ValueError("depth limits must satisfy 0 < min_depth < max_depth")
            if self.voxel_size <= 0:
                raise ValueError("voxel_size must be positive")
            if self.plane_distance_threshold <= 0:
                raise ValueError("plane_distance_threshold must be positive")
            if self.ransac_iterations <= 0:
                raise ValueError("ransac_iterations must be positive")
            if not 0 <= self.object_min_height < self.object_max_height:
                raise ValueError(
                    "object heights must satisfy 0 <= min_height < max_height"
                )
            if self.cluster_eps <= 0:
                raise ValueError("cluster_eps must be positive")
            if self.cluster_min_points <= 0 or self.min_object_pixels <= 0:
                raise ValueError("cluster point thresholds must be positive")
    
    
    @dataclass(frozen=True)
    class DetectedObject:
        """Geometric summary for one accepted point cluster."""
    
        label: int
        pixel_count: int
        voxel_count: int
        centroid_xyz: tuple[float, float, float]
        min_bound_xyz: tuple[float, float, float]
        max_bound_xyz: tuple[float, float, float]
        extent_xyz: tuple[float, float, float]
        centroid_depth_pixel: tuple[float, float]
    
    
    @dataclass(frozen=True)
    class TabletopSegmentationResult:
        """Plane, pixel masks, object geometry, and performance diagnostics."""
    
        plane_model: tuple[float, float, float, float]
        table_mask: np.ndarray
        object_labels: np.ndarray
        objects: tuple[DetectedObject, ...]
        valid_pixel_count: int
        downsampled_point_count: int
        table_voxel_count: int
        candidate_voxel_count: int
        noise_voxel_count: int
        timings_ms: dict[str, float]
    
    
    def _scaled_intrinsics(
        intrinsics: CameraIntrinsics,
        shape: tuple[int, int],
    ) -> tuple[float, float, float, float]:
        height, width = shape
        calibrated_aspect = intrinsics.width / intrinsics.height
        actual_aspect = width / height
        if not np.isclose(actual_aspect, calibrated_aspect, rtol=1e-3):
            raise ValueError(
                f"depth shape {shape} is incompatible with calibrated size "
                f"({intrinsics.height}, {intrinsics.width})"
            )
    
        scale_x = width / intrinsics.width
        scale_y = height / intrinsics.height
        fx = intrinsics.fx * scale_x
        fy = intrinsics.fy * scale_y
        cx = (intrinsics.cx + 0.5) * scale_x - 0.5
        cy = (intrinsics.cy + 0.5) * scale_y - 0.5
        return fx, fy, cx, cy
    
    
    def _as_float_tuple(values: np.ndarray) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
        return tuple(float(value) for value in values)  # type: ignore[return-value]
    
    
    def segment_tabletop_objects(
        depth_meters: np.ndarray,
        intrinsics: CameraIntrinsics,
        parameters: TabletopSegmentationParameters | None = None,
    ) -> TabletopSegmentationResult:
        """Separate a dominant support plane and cluster objects above it.
    
        The table normal is oriented toward the camera origin. Consequently,
        positive signed distances point from the table toward the camera, which is
        the expected side for objects resting on a visible tabletop.
        """
    
        params = parameters or TabletopSegmentationParameters()
        params.validate()
    
        depth = np.asarray(depth_meters, dtype=np.float32)
        if depth.ndim != 2:
            raise ValueError(f"depth_meters must be a 2-D array, got {depth.shape}")
    
        total_started = perf_counter()
        timings: dict[str, float] = {}
    
        stage_started = perf_counter()
        valid_mask = (
            np.isfinite(depth)
            & (depth >= params.min_depth)
            & (depth <= params.max_depth)
        )
        flat_pixel_indices = np.flatnonzero(valid_mask.ravel())
        if len(flat_pixel_indices) < 3:
            raise ValueError("fewer than three depth pixels survive the depth limits")
    
        height, width = depth.shape
        pixel_y, pixel_x = np.unravel_index(flat_pixel_indices, depth.shape)
        z = depth.ravel()[flat_pixel_indices]
        fx, fy, cx, cy = _scaled_intrinsics(intrinsics, depth.shape)
        points = np.column_stack(
            (
                (pixel_x.astype(np.float32) - cx) * z / fx,
                (pixel_y.astype(np.float32) - cy) * z / fy,
                z,
            )
        ).astype(np.float64, copy=False)
        timings["unproject"] = (perf_counter() - stage_started) * 1000
    
        stage_started = perf_counter()
        full_cloud = o3d.geometry.PointCloud()
        full_cloud.points = o3d.utility.Vector3dVector(points)
        margin = params.voxel_size * 0.5
        min_bound = points.min(axis=0) - margin
        max_bound = points.max(axis=0) + margin
        down_cloud, _, trace = full_cloud.voxel_down_sample_and_trace(
            params.voxel_size,
            min_bound,
            max_bound,
            False,
        )
        down_points = np.asarray(down_cloud.points)
        if len(down_points) < 3:
            raise ValueError("fewer than three points remain after voxel downsampling")
        timings["downsample"] = (perf_counter() - stage_started) * 1000
    
        stage_started = perf_counter()
        o3d.utility.random.seed(params.random_seed)
        raw_plane, plane_inliers = down_cloud.segment_plane(
            distance_threshold=params.plane_distance_threshold,
            ransac_n=3,
            num_iterations=params.ransac_iterations,
        )
        plane = np.asarray(raw_plane, dtype=np.float64)
        normal_length = float(np.linalg.norm(plane[:3]))
        if not np.isfinite(normal_length) or normal_length <= 0:
            raise RuntimeError("RANSAC returned an invalid plane model")
        plane /= normal_length
    
        # The camera is at the origin. Make its signed distance non-negative so
        # objects resting on the visible side of the table have positive height.
        if plane[3] < 0:
            plane = -plane
        timings["plane_ransac"] = (perf_counter() - stage_started) * 1000
    
        stage_started = perf_counter()
        signed_down_distances = down_points @ plane[:3] + plane[3]
        candidate_down_indices = np.flatnonzero(
            (signed_down_distances >= params.object_min_height)
            & (signed_down_distances <= params.object_max_height)
        )
        candidate_cloud = down_cloud.select_by_index(candidate_down_indices.tolist())
        timings["height_filter"] = (perf_counter() - stage_started) * 1000
    
        stage_started = perf_counter()
        if len(candidate_down_indices) == 0:
            raw_candidate_labels = np.empty(0, dtype=np.int32)
        else:
            raw_candidate_labels = np.asarray(
                candidate_cloud.cluster_dbscan(
                    eps=params.cluster_eps,
                    min_points=params.cluster_min_points,
                    print_progress=False,
                ),
                dtype=np.int32,
            )
        timings["dbscan"] = (perf_counter() - stage_started) * 1000
    
        stage_started = perf_counter()
        # Map each clustered voxel back through Open3D's trace to the original
        # point list. Values remain -1 for rejected points and DBSCAN noise.
        point_raw_labels = np.full(len(points), -1, dtype=np.int32)
        voxel_counts: dict[int, int] = {}
        for candidate_offset, raw_label in enumerate(raw_candidate_labels):
            if raw_label < 0:
                continue
            down_index = int(candidate_down_indices[candidate_offset])
            source_indices = np.asarray(trace[down_index], dtype=np.int64)
            point_raw_labels[source_indices] = raw_label
            voxel_counts[int(raw_label)] = voxel_counts.get(int(raw_label), 0) + 1
    
        accepted: list[tuple[int, np.ndarray, float]] = []
        for raw_label in np.unique(point_raw_labels[point_raw_labels >= 0]):
            member_indices = np.flatnonzero(point_raw_labels == raw_label)
            if len(member_indices) < params.min_object_pixels:
                continue
            mean_pixel_x = float(pixel_x[member_indices].mean())
            accepted.append((int(raw_label), member_indices, mean_pixel_x))
        accepted.sort(key=lambda item: item[2])
    
        point_labels = np.full(len(points), -1, dtype=np.int32)
        objects: list[DetectedObject] = []
        for label, (raw_label, member_indices, _) in enumerate(accepted):
            point_labels[member_indices] = label
            member_points = points[member_indices]
            min_xyz = member_points.min(axis=0)
            max_xyz = member_points.max(axis=0)
            objects.append(
                DetectedObject(
                    label=label,
                    pixel_count=len(member_indices),
                    voxel_count=voxel_counts[raw_label],
                    centroid_xyz=_as_float_tuple(member_points.mean(axis=0)),
                    min_bound_xyz=_as_float_tuple(min_xyz),
                    max_bound_xyz=_as_float_tuple(max_xyz),
                    extent_xyz=_as_float_tuple(max_xyz - min_xyz),
                    centroid_depth_pixel=(
                        float(pixel_x[member_indices].mean()),
                        float(pixel_y[member_indices].mean()),
                    ),
                )
            )
    
        signed_full_distances = points @ plane[:3] + plane[3]
        point_table_mask = np.abs(signed_full_distances) <= params.plane_distance_threshold
        table_mask = np.zeros(depth.size, dtype=bool)
        table_mask[flat_pixel_indices] = point_table_mask
        table_mask = table_mask.reshape(depth.shape)
    
        object_labels = np.full(depth.size, -1, dtype=np.int32)
        object_labels[flat_pixel_indices] = point_labels
        object_labels = object_labels.reshape(depth.shape)
        timings["label_mapping"] = (perf_counter() - stage_started) * 1000
        timings["total"] = (perf_counter() - total_started) * 1000
    
        return TabletopSegmentationResult(
            plane_model=tuple(float(value) for value in plane),  # type: ignore[arg-type]
            table_mask=table_mask,
            object_labels=object_labels,
            objects=tuple(objects),
            valid_pixel_count=len(points),
            downsampled_point_count=len(down_points),
            table_voxel_count=len(plane_inliers),
            candidate_voxel_count=len(candidate_down_indices),
            noise_voxel_count=int(np.count_nonzero(raw_candidate_labels < 0)),
            timings_ms=timings,
        )

    """Browse a recorded RGB-D feed with classical tabletop segmentation.
    
    Example::
    
        python tabletop_segmentation_demo.py recordings/20260924_113104.db3
    
    The original ``rgbd_db3_viewer.py`` remains independent of this experiment.
    """
    
    from __future__ import annotations
    
    import argparse
    from pathlib import Path
    from time import perf_counter
    
    import cv2
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    import numpy as np
    from matplotlib.axes import Axes
    
    from rgbd_db3_reader import DepthColorProjector, RGBDDB3Reader, RGBDFrame
    from rgbd_tabletop_segmentation import (
        TabletopSegmentationParameters,
        TabletopSegmentationResult,
        segment_tabletop_objects,
    )
    
    
    OBJECT_COLORS = np.asarray(
        [
            (31, 119, 180),
            (255, 127, 14),
            (44, 160, 44),
            (214, 39, 40),
            (148, 103, 189),
            (140, 86, 75),
            (227, 119, 194),
            (188, 189, 34),
            (23, 190, 207),
            (255, 187, 120),
            (152, 223, 138),
            (255, 152, 150),
        ],
        dtype=np.uint8,
    )
    TABLE_COLOR = np.asarray((180, 180, 180), dtype=np.uint8)
    
    
    def _colorize_depth_labels(
        labels: np.ndarray,
        table_mask: np.ndarray,
    ) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
        overlay = np.zeros((*labels.shape, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
        visible = table_mask.copy()
        overlay[table_mask] = TABLE_COLOR
        for label in np.unique(labels[labels >= 0]):
            mask = labels == label
            overlay[mask] = OBJECT_COLORS[int(label) % len(OBJECT_COLORS)]
            visible |= mask
        return overlay, visible
    
    
    def _project_overlay_to_color(
        result: TabletopSegmentationResult,
        projector: DepthColorProjector,
        color_shape: tuple[int, int],
    ) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
        color_height, color_width = color_shape
        overlay = np.zeros((color_height, color_width, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
        visible = np.zeros((color_height, color_width), dtype=bool)
    
        source_labels = result.object_labels.ravel()
        source_table = result.table_mask.ravel()
        source_indices = projector.color_to_depth.ravel()
        has_source = source_indices >= 0
    
        projected_labels = np.full(source_indices.shape, -1, dtype=np.int32)
        projected_table = np.zeros(source_indices.shape, dtype=bool)
        projected_labels[has_source] = source_labels[source_indices[has_source]]
        projected_table[has_source] = source_table[source_indices[has_source]]
        projected_labels = projected_labels.reshape(color_shape)
        projected_table = projected_table.reshape(color_shape)
    
        # A depth sample covers several pixels at the higher color resolution.
        # Dilating individual masks produces a readable overlay without changing
        # the calibrated depth-to-color projection itself.
        kernel = np.ones((3, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
        table_dilated = cv2.dilate(projected_table.astype(np.uint8), kernel) != 0
        overlay[table_dilated] = TABLE_COLOR
        visible |= table_dilated
        for label in np.unique(projected_labels[projected_labels >= 0]):
            mask = cv2.dilate(
                (projected_labels == label).astype(np.uint8), kernel
            ) != 0
            overlay[mask] = OBJECT_COLORS[int(label) % len(OBJECT_COLORS)]
            visible |= mask
        return overlay, visible
    
    
    def _blend(image: np.ndarray, overlay: np.ndarray, mask: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        base = image
        if base.ndim == 2:
            base = np.repeat(base[..., None], 3, axis=2)
        if base.shape[2] == 4:
            base = base[:, :, :3]
        base = base.astype(np.uint8, copy=True)
        base[mask] = np.rint(0.55 * base[mask] + 0.45 * overlay[mask]).astype(np.uint8)
        return base
    
    
    def _print_result(frame: RGBDFrame, result: TabletopSegmentationResult) -> None:
        a, b, c, d = result.plane_model
        timings = ", ".join(
            f"{name}={duration:.1f} ms" for name, duration in result.timings_ms.items()
        )
        print(
            f"frame {frame.index}: {len(result.objects)} objects | "
            f"valid={result.valid_pixel_count:,}, "
            f"voxels={result.downsampled_point_count:,}, "
            f"table={result.table_voxel_count:,}, "
            f"candidates={result.candidate_voxel_count:,}, "
            f"noise={result.noise_voxel_count:,}"
        )
        print(f"  plane: {a:+.4f}x {b:+.4f}y {c:+.4f}z {d:+.4f} = 0")
        print(f"  timing: {timings}")
        for obj in result.objects:
            x, y, z = obj.centroid_xyz
            ex, ey, ez = obj.extent_xyz
            print(
                f"  object {obj.label}: pixels={obj.pixel_count:,}, "
                f"voxels={obj.voxel_count:,}, center=({x:.3f}, {y:.3f}, {z:.3f}) m, "
                f"AABB=({ex:.3f}, {ey:.3f}, {ez:.3f}) m"
            )
    
    
    def _draw_result(
        frame: RGBDFrame,
        result: TabletopSegmentationResult,
        axes: np.ndarray,
        projector: DepthColorProjector,
    ) -> float:
        if frame.color is None or frame.depth_meters is None:
            raise ValueError("the demo requires paired color and depth frames")
    
        projection_started = perf_counter()
        projector.build(frame.depth_meters, frame.color.shape[:2])
        color_overlay, color_mask = _project_overlay_to_color(
            result, projector, frame.color.shape[:2]
        )
        projection_ms = (perf_counter() - projection_started) * 1000
    
        depth_overlay, depth_mask = _colorize_depth_labels(
            result.object_labels, result.table_mask
        )
        segmented_depth = np.zeros_like(depth_overlay)
        segmented_depth[depth_mask] = depth_overlay[depth_mask]
    
        for axis in axes:
            axis.clear()
            axis.axis("off")
    
        axes[0].imshow(_blend(frame.color, color_overlay, color_mask))
        axes[0].set_title("Calibrated color overlay")
    
        axes[1].imshow(
            np.ma.masked_less_equal(frame.depth_meters, 0),
            cmap="turbo",
            vmin=0.25,
            vmax=2.0,
        )
        axes[1].imshow(depth_overlay, alpha=np.where(depth_mask, 0.50, 0.0))
        axes[1].set_title("Depth + table/object masks")
    
        axes[2].imshow(segmented_depth)
        axes[2].set_title(f"{len(result.objects)} object clusters")
        for obj in result.objects:
            u, v = obj.centroid_depth_pixel
            axes[2].text(
                u,
                v,
                str(obj.label),
                ha="center",
                va="center",
                color="white",
                fontsize=10,
                fontweight="bold",
                bbox={"facecolor": "black", "alpha": 0.7, "edgecolor": "none"},
            )
    
        axes[0].figure.suptitle(
            f"Frame {frame.index} | segmentation {result.timings_ms['total']:.1f} ms "
            f"| projection/overlay {projection_ms:.1f} ms"
        )
        axes[0].figure.canvas.draw_idle()
        plt.pause(0.001)
        return projection_ms
    
    
    def run_demo(
        bag_path: Path,
        parameters: TabletopSegmentationParameters,
        *,
        initial_frame: int = 0,
        no_gui: bool = False,
    ) -> None:
        with RGBDDB3Reader(bag_path, rotate_clockwise=True) as reader:
            if len(reader) == 0:
                raise ValueError("the recording contains no paired RGB-D frames")
            if not 0 <= initial_frame < len(reader):
                raise ValueError(f"frame must be between 0 and {len(reader) - 1}")
            if reader.depth_intrinsics is None:
                raise ValueError("the recording does not contain depth intrinsics")
    
            projector = reader.make_projector()
            index = initial_frame
            axes: np.ndarray | None = None
            if not no_gui:
                _, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 7))
                plt.show(block=False)
                print("Commands: Enter/n = next, p = previous, <number> = jump, q = quit")
    
            while True:
                reader.seek(index)
                ok, frame = reader.read()
                if not ok or frame is None or frame.depth_meters is None:
                    break
    
                result = segment_tabletop_objects(
                    frame.depth_meters,
                    reader.depth_intrinsics,
                    parameters,
                )
                _print_result(frame, result)
    
                if no_gui:
                    break
                assert axes is not None
                _draw_result(frame, result, axes, projector)
                if not plt.fignum_exists(axes[0].figure.number):
                    break
    
                command = input(f"frame {index}/{len(reader) - 1}> ").strip().lower()
                if command in {"q", "quit", "exit"}:
                    break
                if command in {"", "n", "next"}:
                    index = min(index + 1, len(reader) - 1)
                elif command in {"p", "prev", "previous"}:
                    index = max(index - 1, 0)
                else:
                    try:
                        requested = int(command)
                    except ValueError:
                        print("Unknown command. Use Enter/n, p, a frame number, or q.")
                        continue
                    if 0 <= requested < len(reader):
                        index = requested
                    else:
                        print(f"Frame must be between 0 and {len(reader) - 1}.")
    
        plt.close("all")
    
    
    def _positive_float(value: str) -> float:
        number = float(value)
        if number <= 0:
            raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError("must be positive")
        return number
    
    
    def parse_args() -> argparse.Namespace:
        parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
            description="Segment tabletop objects in a recorded RGB-D stream."
        )
        parser.add_argument(
            "bag",
            nargs="?",
            type=Path,
            default=Path("recordings/20260924_113104.db3"),
            help="recording path (default: recordings/20260924_113104.db3)",
        )
        parser.add_argument("--frame", type=int, default=0, help="initial frame index")
        parser.add_argument(
            "--no-gui",
            action="store_true",
            help="process one frame, print diagnostics, and exit",
        )
        parser.add_argument("--min-depth", type=float, default=0.25)
        parser.add_argument("--max-depth", type=float, default=2.0)
        parser.add_argument("--voxel-size", type=_positive_float, default=0.005)
        parser.add_argument("--plane-threshold", type=_positive_float, default=0.010)
        parser.add_argument("--ransac-iterations", type=int, default=1_000)
        parser.add_argument("--object-min-height", type=float, default=0.010)
        parser.add_argument("--object-max-height", type=float, default=0.40)
        parser.add_argument("--cluster-eps", type=_positive_float, default=0.020)
        parser.add_argument("--cluster-min-points", type=int, default=20)
        parser.add_argument("--min-object-pixels", type=int, default=100)
        return parser.parse_args()
    
    
    def main() -> None:
        args = parse_args()
        parameters = TabletopSegmentationParameters(
            min_depth=args.min_depth,
            max_depth=args.max_depth,
            voxel_size=args.voxel_size,
            plane_distance_threshold=args.plane_threshold,
            ransac_iterations=args.ransac_iterations,
            object_min_height=args.object_min_height,
            object_max_height=args.object_max_height,
            cluster_eps=args.cluster_eps,
            cluster_min_points=args.cluster_min_points,
            min_object_pixels=args.min_object_pixels,
        )
        run_demo(
            args.bag,
            parameters,
            initial_frame=args.frame,
            no_gui=args.no_gui,
        )
    
    
    if __name__ == "__main__":
        main()

## Assistant

The first real run works end to end, but the raw defaults produce 17 clusters—several clearly too small to be meaningful objects, and two large merged regions. That is exactly why I’m not stopping at “it executes.” I’m rendering the actual overlay now, then I’ll tune only defensible filters and preserve the raw diagnostics so failure modes stay visible. Current measured segmentation time is about 522 ms, dominated by traceable voxel downsampling and label propagation.

## Assistant

The actual image exposed the important scene-specific trap: the wall is the globally largest plane. I corrected that by making support-plane fitting explicitly use the lower calibrated image region, then restricting object candidates to the tabletop workspace. The result now isolates the five visible medicine boxes on frame 0; I’m validating that this stays stable across the entire 46-frame recording and checking the final overlay and dependency state.

- Number: jump to frame

The display contains:

- Calibrated cluster overlay on RGB
- Depth with table and object masks
- Isolated object clusters, each assigned a deterministic color and number
- Plane equation, point counts, object centroids, dimensions, heights, and timing in the terminal

The implementation uses Open3D’s traceable voxel downsampling, RANSAC plane fitting, and DBSCAN clustering. [Open3D point-cloud documentation](https://www.open3d.org/docs/latest/tutorial/geometry/pointcloud.html)

An important correction emerged during testing: the wall, not the table, is the globally largest plane. The detector therefore fits the support plane within the lower part of the calibrated image and restricts object searching to the tabletop region. Both regions are configurable.

    ### Segment plane with RANSAC and visualize inliers/outliers
    
    Source: https://github.com/isl-org/open3d/blob/main/docs/jupyter/geometry/pointcloud.ipynb
    
    Loads a sample point cloud, uses `pcd.segment_plane` with `distance_threshold=0.01`, `ransac_n=3`, and `num_iterations=1000` to find the largest plane. The inliers are colored red and both inlier and outlier clouds are visualized with `draw_geometries`.
    
    ```python
    pcd_point_cloud = o3d.data.PCDPointCloud()
    pcd = o3d.io.read_point_cloud(pcd_point_cloud.path)
    
    plane_model, inliers = pcd.segment_plane(distance_threshold=0.01,
                                             ransac_n=3,
                                             num_iterations=1000)
    [a, b, c, d] = plane_model
    print(f"Plane equation: {a:.2f}x + {b:.2f}y + {c:.2f}z + {d:.2f} = 0")
    
    inlier_cloud = pcd.select_by_index(inliers)
    inlier_cloud.paint_uniform_color([1.0, 0, 0])
    outlier_cloud = pcd.select_by_index(inliers, invert=True)
    o3d.visualization.draw_geometries([inlier_cloud, outlier_cloud],
                                      zoom=0.8,
                                      front=[-0.4999, -0.1659, -0.8499],
                                      lookat=[2.1813, 2.0619, 2.0999],
                                      up=[0.1204, -0.9852, 0.1215])
    ```

    ### Compute point cloud distance with compute_point_cloud_distance
    
    Source: https://github.com/isl-org/open3d/blob/main/docs/jupyter/geometry/pointcloud.ipynb
    
    Loads a demo point cloud, crops it with a selection polygon, computes distances from the original point cloud to the cropped chair, and removes points closer than 0.01 to visualize the difference. Useful for computing Chamfer distance or comparing point clouds.
    
    ```python
    # Load data
    demo_crop_data = o3d.data.DemoCropPointCloud()
    pcd = o3d.io.read_point_cloud(demo_crop_data.point_cloud_path)
    vol = o3d.visualization.read_selection_polygon_volume(demo_crop_data.cropped_json_path)
    chair = vol.crop_point_cloud(pcd)
    
    dists = pcd.compute_point_cloud_distance(chair)
    dists = np.asarray(dists)
    ind = np.where(dists > 0.01)[0]
    pcd_without_chair = pcd.select_by_index(ind)
    o3d.visualization.draw_geometries([pcd_without_chair],
                                      zoom=0.3412,
                                      front=[0.4257, -0.2125, -0.8795],
                                      lookat=[2.6172, 2.0475, 1.532],
                                      up=[-0.0694, -0.9768, 0.2024])
    ```
    
    ### Plane segmentation
    
    Source: https://github.com/isl-org/open3d/blob/main/docs/jupyter/t_geometry/pointcloud.ipynb
    
    Open3D also supports segmententation of geometric primitives from point clouds using RANSAC. To find the plane with the largest support in the point cloud, we can use `segment_plane`. The method has four arguments: `distance_threshold` defines the maximum distance a point can have to an estimated plane to be considered an inlier, `ransac_n` defines the number of points that are randomly sampled to estimate a plane, `num_iterations` defines how often a random plane is sampled and verified, and `probability` defined the expected probability of finding the optimal plane. The function then returns the plane as $(a,b,c,d)$ such that for each point $(x,y,z)$ on the plane we have $ax + by + cz + d = 0$. The function further returns a indices of the inlier points.

## Assistant

The fix will not be a bag-specific depth cutoff. I found two large, nearly parallel support-plane candidates in the failing recording: the real table at about 0.355 m perpendicular distance and the bottom structure at about 1.28 m. I’m changing the detector to extract several strong planes, retain only table-like orientations with substantial support, and select the nearest credible support plane. That directly models what the scene contains.

    +    # A scene can contain several parallel horizontal surfaces. In particular,
    +    # some recordings show both the medicine table and a large structure at
    +    # the bottom of the image. Peel off several RANSAC planes, keep substantial
    +    # planes whose normal points mostly along the rotated image's vertical
    +    # axis, and choose the nearest credible one rather than blindly choosing
    +    # the globally largest plane.
    +    candidates: list[tuple[np.ndarray, int]] = []
    +    remaining_plane_cloud = plane_fit_cloud
    +    for candidate_index in range(params.plane_candidate_count):
    +        if len(remaining_plane_cloud.points) < 3:
    +            break
    +        o3d.utility.random.seed(params.random_seed + candidate_index)
    +        raw_plane, inliers = remaining_plane_cloud.segment_plane(
    +            distance_threshold=params.plane_distance_threshold,
    +            ransac_n=3,
    +            num_iterations=params.ransac_iterations,
    +        )
    +        if len(inliers) < 3:
    +            break
    +        candidate = np.asarray(raw_plane, dtype=np.float64)
    +        normal_length = float(np.linalg.norm(candidate[:3]))
    +        if np.isfinite(normal_length) and normal_length > 0:
    +            candidate /= normal_length
    +            # The camera is at the origin. Positive d orients the normal from
    +            # the support surface toward the camera.
    +            if candidate[3] < 0:

    +            if (

## Assistant

A full-sequence check found one remaining pattern: a small cluster intermittently appears at the extreme right and always touches pixel column 479, while every medicine cluster is fully contained in the frame. I’m adding a standard reliability rule: reject clusters clipped by the image boundary, with an exposed margin setting. Partial boundary clusters cannot yield trustworthy dimensions or grasps anyway.

## Assistant

The boundary rule removed most of the artifact, but a few frames contain an internally disconnected fragment just inside the edge. I’ve therefore made the already implicit workspace assumption explicit: object candidates are accepted only within a configurable horizontal ROI (`5%–90%` of depth-image width by default). This is preferable to pretending every above-plane point anywhere in the room is a grasp target. The real boxes in both recordings remain well inside that region.

## Assistant

Fixed. The failing recording now detects only the objects on the medicine table; the false lower-right detections are gone.

Root cause: Open3D’s `segment_plane` returns the plane with the strongest support. This recording contains a second large, parallel surface near the bottom, so the original single-plane approach selected the wrong surface. [Open3D plane segmentation](https://github.com/isl-org/open3d/blob/main/docs/jupyter/geometry/pointcloud.ipynb)

Changes:

- Extracts up to four plane candidates.
- Keeps planes with a plausible tabletop orientation and substantial support.
- Selects the nearest credible support plane.
- Rejects clusters clipped by an image boundary.
- Adds a configurable horizontal workspace ROI.
- Leaves `rgbd_db3_viewer.py` unchanged.

Validation:

- `20260924_113006.db3`: all 97 frames select the correct plane, consistently at `0.353–0.357 m`.
- No detected centroid appears in the erroneous corner anymore.
- The default bag continues to detect five objects throughout.
- The failing bag generally reports four clusters because the two rightmost boxes form one depth-connected component. Occasionally DBSCAN separates them into five. Splitting touching boxes is the next distinct problem.

Run normally:

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe .\tabletop_segmentation_demo.py `
    .\recordings\20260924_113006.db3
```

New adjustable parameters include:

```text
--plane-roi-top
--object-roi-left
--object-roi-right
--border-margin-pixels
```

To allow detections at the extreme right in a future setup:

```powershell
--object-roi-right 1.0 --border-margin-pixels -1
```

    ### Applying Distance Transform
    
    Source: https://docs.opencv.org/4.13.0/d2/dbd/tutorial_distance_transform.html
    
    Calculates the distance transform of a binary image. DIST_L2 uses the Euclidean distance, and the mask size of 3 is typical for this operation.
    
    ```python
    dist = cv.distanceTransform(bw, cv.DIST_L2, 3)
    ```
    
    --------------------------------
    
    ### Normalizing and Thresholding Distance Transform
    
    Source: https://docs.opencv.org/4.13.0/d2/dbd/tutorial_distance_transform.html
    
    Normalizes the distance transform image to the range [0.0, 1.0] for visualization and then applies a binary threshold to identify potential peaks.
    
    ```python
    # Normalize the distance image for range = {0.0, 1.0}
    # so we can visualize and threshold it
    cv.normalize(dist, dist, 0, 1.0, cv.NORM_MINMAX)
    _, dist = cv.threshold(dist, 0.4, 1.0, cv.THRESH_BINARY)
    ```
    
    --------------------------------
    
    ### connectedComponents
    
    Source: https://docs.opencv.org/4.13.0/javadoc/org/opencv/imgproc/Imgproc.html
    
    Computes the connected components labeled image of a boolean image with 4 or 8-way connectivity. Returns N, the total number of labels [0, N-1] where 0 represents the background label.
    
    ```APIDOC
    ## connectedComponents
    
    ### Description
    Computes the connected components labeled image of boolean image image with 4 or 8 way connectivity - returns N, the total number of labels [0, N-1] where 0 represents the background label.
    
    ### Method
    `public static int connectedComponents(Mat image, Mat labels, int connectivity, int ltype)`
    
    ### Parameters
    #### Path Parameters
    - **image** (Mat) - the 8-bit single-channel image to be labeled
    - **labels** (Mat) - destination labeled image
    - **connectivity** (int) - 8 or 4 for 8-way or 4-way connectivity respectively
    - **ltype** (int) - output image label type. Currently CV_32S and CV_16U are supported.
    ```
    
    --------------------------------
    
    ### Watershed Algorithm for Image Segmentation
    
    Source: https://docs.opencv.org/4.13.0/javadoc/org/opencv/imgproc/Imgproc.html
    
    Performs marker-based image segmentation using the watershed algorithm. Requires pre-defined markers to outline regions.
    
    ```Java
    public static void watershed(Mat image, Mat markers)
    ```
    
    ### Code
    
    Source: https://docs.opencv.org/4.13.0/d7/d1c/tutorial_js_watershed.html
    
    The tutorial demonstrates using the Distance Transform with the watershed algorithm to segment touching objects, using a coins image as an example. It involves steps like Otsu's binarization to estimate coin locations, morphological opening to remove noise, and morphological closing to fill holes. The process also includes finding sure foreground and background regions using erosion and dilation, respectively, to handle touching objects.
